description: Interested in software and coding to create a positive impact and autonomous workflows.
summary:
One Mars or Moon mission can need several Earth test sites. We built AnalogForge to help rover teams find places to rehearse each capability and decide what to measure there. Teams enter a mission target and rover requirements. AnalogForge compares terrain, maps candidate sites, and produces downloadable field briefs with test benchmarks and, where available, modeled routes and checkpoints.

To demonstrate our approach, we used NASA elevation data to compare a region within Gale Crater on Mars with four areas north of Flagstaff, Arizona. Two met our threshold for a similar mix of slopes, making them candidates for further scouting. The public demo uses labeled practice data to show how a team can turn a shortlist into a rover test plan.

AnalogForge helps field teams decide where to scout, what to test, and which requirements still need evidence before they commit time and equipment to a field trial.
details:
A rover’s wheels, battery, and sampling system all have different jobs. The best place to test each one can be different, too. A hillside with the right slopes might be ideal for testing how the rover climbs. A long, continuous stretch of ground might be better for measuring how much battery remains after a drive. We built AnalogForge to put those places together into one test plan for a Mars or Moon mission.

The creative part is how we choose the sites. Each recommendation starts with a capability the mission depends on and asks what kind of terrain would let the team test it. You choose a target, describe your rover, and tell AnalogForge what it needs to do. You review the proposed tests and benchmarks, then explore a map of Earth sites that could support them. Changing the rover’s features or the mission’s goals can change the recommended sites, even when the target stays the same. Each site has a reason for being on the map, and the downloadable field guide spells out what to test there, what to measure, and what result would meet the benchmark. When a modeled route is available, the guide includes a start point and checkpoints. It also shows what still needs to be checked in the field.

One way we checked the approach was to compare NASA elevation maps of Gale Crater on Mars with four areas north of Flagstaff, Arizona. Two had a similar enough mix of slopes to be worth scouting. Our public demo uses labeled practice data so anyone can see the rest of the process, from setting rover requirements to downloading a test plan.

We built the website with React and TypeScript, used Python to work with the terrain maps, and hosted it on Microsoft Azure. We want rover teams to know why they’re going to each site, what they’re there to learn, and how they’ll tell whether the rover did what the mission needs.

We used OpenAI Codex and Claude Code to help build, debug, and review parts of the project. In AnalogForge, AI can turn a plain-language mission description into proposed tests and benchmarks. The user reviews those proposals before starting a run. The terrain scores come from calculations on the elevation data using the accepted criteria. The app keeps missing evidence visible so teams can see what still needs checking.
